standard.title: Economic Interdependence
standard.description: how economic decision-making involves the interdependence of consumers, businesses, the financial sector and government
standard.prior_knowledge: From AC9HE9K01 (direct predecessor): Australia's financial sector — its structure, functions, products and global role. From Y8: market mechanisms and price signals (AC9HE8K01), business adaptation (AC9HE8K02). Students understand how individual actors operate in markets but have not yet analysed how their decisions are mutually dependent within local, national and global economic systems.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students explain how economic decision-making involves the interdependence of consumers, businesses, the financial sector and government.

nodes.label: The circular flow of economic decision-making
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain how consumers, businesses, the financial sector and government play interdependent roles in economic decision-making within local, national and global contexts.
nodes.minimum_width: Describe how two of the four actors (e.g. consumers and businesses) make interdependent decisions, using one concrete example.
nodes.typical_width: Explain the interdependent nature of economic decision-making across all four actors — consumers (purchasing goods and services), businesses (organising production and distribution), the financial sector (facilitating investment and credit), and government (setting rules, collecting taxes, providing services) — within local, national and global contexts. Use examples showing how a decision by one actor affects others.
wider: Trace how a change in consumer sentiment (e.g. reduced spending during economic uncertainty) flows through all four actors — affecting business revenue, financial sector lending, and government tax receipts
Compare how the four-actor interdependence operates differently at local (community business), national (ASX-listed firm) and global (transnational corporation) scales
Examine how First Nations community enterprises operate within this interdependence, including distinctive relationships with government and community consumers
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who understand each actor in isolation but not interdependence will be unable to analyse how decisions propagate through the system — the core demand of this descriptor and a prerequisite for understanding globalisation effects in subsequent nodes.

response_modes.reason: The circular flow model requires students to trace decision chains across actors. A visual diagram of actor relationships with explicit arrows showing decision flows helps students reason about interdependence rather than treating actors as independent.
Multiple scale contexts (local, national, global) prevent students from thinking interdependence only operates at one level — a common misconception that limits transfer to globalisation analysis.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The four-actor model at different scales (local, national, global) offers rich comparative contexts. First Nations community enterprises add a culturally significant variant that reveals how the model's assumptions can be challenged by alternative economic relationships.
success_criteria: Names all four actors in economic decision-making
Explains, using an example, how a decision by one actor affects at least one other actor
Uses terms such as 'interdependence', 'consumer', 'financial sector' correctly

nodes.label: Globalisation and supply chains
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain how globalisation supports transnational corporations using supply chains, and can describe advantages and disadvantages for businesses, workers and consumers.
nodes.minimum_width: Explain what a supply chain is and identify one advantage and one disadvantage of globalised supply chains for either businesses, workers or consumers.
nodes.typical_width: Explain how globalisation enables transnational corporations to use supply chains to develop, produce and deliver products or services across countries. Explain advantages for businesses (cost reduction, market access, specialisation), workers (employment, skill development) and consumers (lower prices, product variety), and disadvantages for each (loss of local manufacturing, labour exploitation, dependency risks, price volatility). Use at least one named example.
wider: Investigate a specific Australian industry (e.g. clothing retail, electronics, agriculture) to trace its global supply chain and identify which advantages and disadvantages are most significant for Australian stakeholders
Examine the disruption to global supply chains during COVID-19 and explain what this revealed about the risks of highly interdependent global production systems
Analyse how ethical consumerism (e.g. Fair Trade, country-of-origin labelling) represents a consumer response to the disadvantages of globalised supply chains

response_modes.reason: Students need specific named examples of transnational corporations and supply chains to answer 'analyse implications' type tasks. Building a repertoire of 2-3 concrete cases before analysing implications prevents vague generalisations.

success_criteria: Explains what a supply chain is and how transnational corporations use them
Identifies at least one advantage and one disadvantage of globalised supply chains for a named stakeholder group
Uses terms such as 'globalisation', 'supply chain', 'transnational corporation'

nodes.label: Implications of global economic interdependence for Australia
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can analyse implications of interdependence within the global economy for Australian consumers, workers and businesses, including costs and disruption risks.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify one implication of global economic interdependence for Australian consumers or businesses (e.g. cost effects from overseas regulation changes or supply disruptions).
nodes.typical_width: Analyse the implications of global economic interdependence for Australian consumers (product costs, price fluctuations, access to variety), workers (employment in trade-exposed industries, skill demands) and businesses (cost structures, supply reliability, regulatory exposure). Include examples of how changes to regulations, economic conditions or disruptions in another country affect Australian actors.
wider: Investigate how changes to Chinese economic policy or consumer preferences have affected Australian export industries (e.g. iron ore, education, agricultural exports) and trace implications for workers and businesses
Examine how trade sanctions or geopolitical tensions (e.g. trade disputes between major economies) create uncertainty for Australian businesses operating in global markets
Analyse how digital trade and platform economy companies (e.g. streaming services, ride-sharing) have created new forms of global economic interdependence affecting Australian consumers and workers

response_modes.reason: The implications vary significantly by stakeholder group and industry. Multiple Australian case contexts (manufacturing, agriculture, services, digital economy) prevent students from generalising from one sector to all.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: Australia's highly trade-exposed economy provides rich real cases — China-Australia trade tensions, COVID supply disruptions, digital platform economy — where students can trace interdependence implications through to named Australian stakeholders.
success_criteria: Identifies at least two implications of global economic interdependence for Australian actors
Explains the mechanism by which a change in another country's conditions affects Australian consumers, workers or businesses
Distinguishes implications for different stakeholder groups (consumers vs workers vs businesses)

nodes.label: How national economic conditions affect other nations
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain, using examples, how changes to one nation's economic conditions affect other nations through interdependent relationships.
nodes.minimum_width: Using one example, explain how a change in one country's economic condition (e.g. rising unemployment) affects another country's economy (e.g. reduced demand for exports).
nodes.typical_width: Explain how changes to a nation's economic conditions — unemployment, interest rates, consumer demand, economic growth — affect other nations through trade and financial interdependence. Use the elaboration example (rising unemployment → reduced consumer demand → lower imports → affected export revenues in other countries) and at least one additional example showing different causal chains. Connect to how Australia is affected by conditions in major trading partners.
wider: Investigate how the Global Financial Crisis (2008) spread from the US financial sector to affect economic conditions in countries with different levels of financial integration, including Australia
Examine how China's economic slowdown periods have created ripple effects in Australia's mining sector, housing market and tertiary education — tracing the causal chain for each
Analyse how a rise in US interest rates affects borrowing costs, currency values and investment decisions in countries with different levels of economic interdependence with the US

response_modes.reason: This node integrates interdependence (Node 1), supply chains (Node 2), and Australian implications (Node 3) into an explanation of bidirectional cross-national effects. Students should trace the causal chain explicitly: national condition → mechanism → effect on other nations → effect on Australia.

success_criteria: Explains the causal chain by which a change in one nation's economic conditions affects another nation
Uses a named real example to illustrate the explanation
Connects the explanation to effects on Australian consumers, businesses or workers
